Too many stories to check

Guessing what we never see, four ways: the evidence lower bound and approximate inference
Yuwen Huang

Teaching edition
→ next · ← back · F full screen · H keys
The story

A friend secretly switches coins, and we see only the flips

A friend secretly flips coin A (often heads) or coin B (rarely heads). The friend usually keeps the same coin but sometimes switches.

We see only heads, heads, tails. Which coin made each flip, and what are the friend's habits?

The coins are hidden; we must learn from what we see.

The story · last week

Last week, we guessed the coins and then counted

Guess: find the chance that coin A made each flip. Count: with these guesses, count each coin's heads and the friend's switches. Then repeat.

This loop is EM, expectation–maximization: each round, the guesses and the habits get better.

The story · the problem

To guess well, we must weigh every secret story

To guess the coin of flip 2 exactly, we must weigh every secret story: every choice of coins.

Today's question: how can we guess well when there are too many stories to check?

With few flips we can check every story; with many flips we cannot.

Warm-up

Two ideas from earlier lectures that come back today

1. In Lecture 4, a sum was too large to compute exactly. What did we do instead?
Answer. We drew random examples and averaged them: today's Way 2, act it out.
2. In Week 2, messages were exact on a tree. What goes wrong on a loop?
Answer. It returns, so its news is counted twice: today's Way 4, messages in a circle.

Both ideas return today, as Way 2 and Way 4.

Today's map

One score and four ways to guess when stories are too many

Each way gives up some exactness to gain speed.

Objectives

By the end of today, you can explain five things

1why a score judges a guess without the truththe score

One friend, two coins, four ways to guess.

1 · A score for every guess · Idea

We cannot compute the truth, but we can score any guess

For any guess of the hidden coins, we can compute a score. It is always below the true answer and equals it only for a perfect guess.

A better guess has a higher score, so we can improve a guess without knowing the truth.

1 · A score for every guess · Definition

The score is the evidence lower bound (ELBO)

Four ingredients for our three flips:

  1. the flips, xxx: H, H, T;
  2. the hidden coins, zzz: one secret story, such as A, A, B;
  3. the habits, θ\thetaθ: heads 34\tfrac3443​ for A, 14\tfrac1441​ for B, keep 34\tfrac3443​;
  4. our guess, qqq: a chance for each of the 8 stories.
The score: B(q,θ)=∑zq(z)⋅ln⁡pθ(x,z)q(z)\displaystyle B(q,\theta)=\sum_z q(z)\cdot\ln\frac{p_\theta(x,z)}{q(z)}B(q,θ)=z∑​q(z)⋅lnq(z)pθ​(x,z)​, summed over the 8 stories
Truth = score + gap: ln⁡pθ(x)=B(q,θ)+gap\ln p_\theta(x)=B(q,\theta)+\text{gap}lnpθ​(x)=B(q,θ)+gap; the gap is never negative, and zero only for a perfect guess

So the score is a lower bound on the evidence, the log-chance of the flips: the evidence lower bound (ELBO) (Lecture 5, Lemma 1).

Raising the score closes the gap or improves the habits.

1 · A score for every guess · The loop again

Expectation–maximization raises this score in two steps

Guess step: make the guess qqq as good as possible. Count step: with qqq fixed, choose the habits θ\thetaθ with the best score.

But the best guess weighs every secret story, which is impossible with many flips.

Today: four ways to make the guess step cheap enough to compute.

1 · A score for every guess · Next

Way 1: if the coins form a line, they can pass messages

Each coin depends only on the coin before it (a Markov chain). This assumption lets us avoid listing the stories.

Way 1 gives the exact guess at low cost.

Way 1 · Pass messages along a line · Idea

Coins in a line can pass messages instead of listing stories

The one assumption: the friend chooses each coin from the previous coin only. This is a Markov chain: p(zt∣z1,…,zt−1)=p(zt∣zt−1)p(z_t\mid z_1,\dots,z_{t-1})=p(z_t\mid z_{t-1})p(zt​∣z1​,…,zt−1​)=p(zt​∣zt−1​).

So each coin sends its neighbour a short message that summarizes the flips on its side. We need one pass forward and one pass back.

Because the coins form a Markov chain, two passes replace checking every story.

Way 1 · Pass messages along a line · As a factor graph

The coin game is a chain factor graph

Take our three coins. Each circle is a hidden coin ztz_tzt​, and each square is one habit:

  1. the start: which coin the friend picks first;
  2. keep or switch: how each coin follows the one before;
  3. shows H or shows T: how each coin made its flip xtx_txt​.
Chance of a story = product of the squares: p(z,x)=p(z1) p(x1∣z1)⋅p(z2∣z1) p(x2∣z2)⋅p(z3∣z2) p(x3∣z3)p(z,x)=p(z_1)\,p(x_1\mid z_1)\cdot p(z_2\mid z_1)\,p(x_2\mid z_2)\cdot p(z_3\mid z_2)\,p(x_3\mid z_3)p(z,x)=p(z1​)p(x1​∣z1​)⋅p(z2​∣z1​)p(x2​∣z2​)⋅p(z3​∣z2​)p(x3​∣z3​)

Each coin links only to its neighbours: no loop, so the graph is a tree.

Way 1 · Pass messages along a line · Sum-product

Forward–backward is the sum-product algorithm on this chain

Take the chance that coin 2 is A. Three things reach coin 2; each message sums out the far coin, Lecture 2's rule:

  1. the message from the left: coin 1's news, carried over keep or switch;
  2. coin 2's own flip, H;
  3. the message from the right: coin 3's news, explaining the last flip T.
Messages: α2(z2)=p(x2=H∣z2)∑z1p(z2∣z1) α1(z1)β2(z2)=∑z3p(z3∣z2) p(x3=T∣z3)\color{#0057e7}{\alpha_2(z_2)}=p(x_2{=}\mathrm H\mid z_2)\textstyle\sum_{z_1}p(z_2\mid z_1)\,\alpha_1(z_1)\qquad \color{#c86400}{\beta_2(z_2)}=\textstyle\sum_{z_3}p(z_3\mid z_2)\,p(x_3{=}\mathrm T\mid z_3)α2​(z2​)=p(x2​=H∣z2​)∑z1​​p(z2​∣z1​)α1​(z1​)β2​(z2​)=∑z3​​p(z3​∣z2​)p(x3​=T∣z3​)
Chance coin 2 is A = left ×\times× flip ×\times× right, rescaled: p(z2=A∣x)=α2(A) β2(A) / p(x)p(z_2{=}A\mid x)=\alpha_2(A)\,\beta_2(A)\,/\,p(x)p(z2​=A∣x)=α2​(A)β2​(A)/p(x)

Forward–backward is Lecture 2's sum-product algorithm on a chain.

Way 1 · Pass messages along a line · On our flips

On H, H, T, the two forward–backward messages meet at coin 2

The forward message α2\alpha_2α2​ is the chance of the first flips H, H, ending at coin A or B. The backward message β2\beta_2β2​ is the chance of the last flip T, starting from A or B.

Next: where each of these four numbers comes from, one step at a time.

Way 1 · Pass messages along a line · The starting numbers

The starting numbers are our first guess of the habits

We never see the habits, so EM starts from a first guess θ\thetaθ and improves it each round:

Only a first guess: the count step will replace it.

Multiplying the two messages gives chance 0.75 that coin 2 is A

Way 1 · Pass messages along a line · Learning the habits

We count the habits with the messages' guesses, then repeat

Take coin A's heads chance. The messages say coin A made flips 1, 2, 3 with chances 0.8, 0.75, 0.4 . Count:

  1. heads made by A = 0.8 + 0.75 = 1.55, because only flips 1 and 2 are H;
  2. flips made by A = 0.8 + 0.75 + 0.4 = 1.95;
  3. new heads chance of A = 1.55 ÷ 1.95 ≈ 0.795.
New heads chance of A =∑t: xt=Hp(zt=A∣x)∑tp(zt=A∣x)=\dfrac{\sum_{t:\,x_t=\mathrm H}p(z_t{=}A\mid x)}{\sum_{t}p(z_t{=}A\mid x)}=∑t​p(zt​=A∣x)∑t:xt​=H​p(zt​=A∣x)​; coin B and the keep chance: the same way.

Count with the messages, pass new messages, repeat: this is Baum–Welch, EM for coins in a line.

Way 1 · Pass messages along a line · What we get

Without a cycle, these messages give the exact posterior

The messages gave 0.8, 0.75, 0.4: exactly what listing all 8 stories gives, because

  1. the coins form a line, so the factor graph has no cycle;
  2. so each flip's news reaches a coin by one path: nothing is counted twice.
Forward–backward theorem . On any chain, at every flip ttt,   p(x)=∑zαt(z) βt(z)  \;p(x)=\sum_{z}\alpha_t(z)\,\beta_t(z)\;p(x)=∑z​αt​(z)βt​(z) and   p(zt=z∣x)=αt(z) βt(z)p(x)\;p(z_t{=}z\mid x)=\dfrac{\alpha_t(z)\,\beta_t(z)}{p(x)}p(zt​=z∣x)=p(x)αt​(z)βt​(z)​, exactly.

This is Lecture 2's Theorem 1, sum-product on a tree: no cycle, so every marginal is exact.

With no cycle, each flip is counted once, so the posterior is exact.

Way 1 · Pass messages along a line · The limit

If the line becomes a circle, the messages have no starting point

If coin 3 also depends on coin 1, the coins form a circle, and no first coin exists to start the forward message.

Messages along a line are exact only when the coins really form a Markov chain.

Way 1 · Pass messages along a line · Next

Way 2: when we cannot add up the stories, act them out

As in Lecture 4, instead of adding up every case, we try many cases at random and count.

Way 2 is correct on average but needs many runs.

Way 2 · Act it out · Idea

Replay the game many times and keep the runs that match

  1. Play the friend's game: choose coin 1 at random, keep or switch with the friend's chances, and flip each coin.
  2. Compare: if your flips are H, H, T, keep the run; otherwise, discard it.
  3. Count: among the kept runs, find how often coin 2 was A.

The kept runs appear in the right proportions, so no sum over all stories is needed.

Way 2 · Act it out · Learning the habits

In a kept run we see the coins, so we can simply count

The count step needs each coin's flips and heads . In a kept run we chose the coins ourselves, so we can count them.

  1. Kept run 1, A, A, B over H, H, T : coin A 2 flips, 2 heads; coin B 1 flip, 0 heads; kept once, switched once.
  2. Add the counts over all kept runs: the new habits, as in Baum–Welch's count step , e.g. coin A heads 0.795 .

They agree because kept runs come in the right proportions. This is Monte Carlo EM: acting out replaces the guess step.

Simulate, keep, count, and repeat.

Way 2 · Act it out · The cost

Random runs add error; four times as many runs halve it

Take the chance that coin 2 is A, truly 0.75, counted from the kept runs:

  1. 16 kept runs: typically off by about 0.11;
  2. 64 kept runs, four times as many: off by about 0.05, half as much;
  3. halving it again needs four times as many again.
Typical error, the standard deviation: q (1−q)/m\sqrt{q\,(1-q)/m}q(1−q)/m​, with qqq the true chance and mmm the kept runs

The error falls like one over the square root of the runs: correct on average, but slow.

Way 2 · Act it out · On a circle

No first coin on a circle, so we redraw one coin at a time

Replaying went in order, coin 1, 2, 3. On a circle coin 3 ties back to coin 1: no first coin. Instead:

  1. Keep a current story, say A, A, B. Pick one coin, say coin 2.
  2. Redraw coin 2 from the three things that touch it: coin 1, coin 3 and its own flip H (worked: ).
  3. Repeat round the circle many times, and count how often each coin is A.
In symbols: p(z2∣z1,z3,x2) ∝ p(z2∣z1)⏟move 1→2 p(z3∣z2)⏟move 2→3 p(x2∣z2)⏟its flipp(z_2\mid z_1,z_3,x_2)\ \propto\ \underbrace{p(z_2\mid z_1)}_{\text{move }1\to2}\ \underbrace{p(z_3\mid z_2)}_{\text{move }2\to3}\ \underbrace{p(x_2\mid z_2)}_{\text{its flip}}p(z2​∣z1​,z3​,x2​) ∝ move 1→2p(z2​∣z1​)​​ move 2→3p(z3​∣z2​)​​ its flipp(x2​∣z2​)​​: only the squares touching coin 2.

This is Gibbs sampling from Week 4: in the long run the counts are exact .

Way 2 · Act it out · Next

Way 3: let each coin guess alone, which is fast

Acting out is slow. What if each coin made its own guess, using its neighbours' guesses?

Way 3 gives up a little accuracy for much more speed.

Way 3 · Everyone guesses alone · Idea

Mean field approximates the joint by a product

  1. The truth p(z∣x)p(z\mid x)p(z∣x) is one table over all 8 stories: 7 free numbers.
  2. Mean field replaces it by a product of three one-coin tables: q(z)=q1(z1) q2(z2) q3(z3)q(z)=q_1(z_1)\,q_2(z_2)\,q_3(z_3)q(z)=q1​(z1​)q2​(z2​)q3​(z3​), 3 numbers.
  3. The price: a product cannot say "coins 1 and 2 agree". Each coin's table is chosen using the other two .

Joint table → product of small tables: cheap, but no links between coins.

Way 3 · Everyone guesses alone · Definition

Among all products, choose the one with the best score

Mean field: max⁡q1,q2,q3 B(q1q2q3,θ)\displaystyle\max_{q_1,q_2,q_3}\ B\big(q_1q_2q_3,\theta\big)q1​,q2​,q3​max​ B(q1​q2​q3​,θ): the product with the largest score .

The simplest variational inference: guessing becomes maximizing a score over a family, here the products.

Three numbers instead of a table over every story.

Way 3 · Everyone guesses alone · Theorem A

Theorem A: guessing the coins is climbing the score

Theorem A (variational principle). For every guess qqq: ln⁡p(x)=B(q)+KL(q ∥ p(z∣x))\ln p(x)=B(q)+\mathrm{KL}\big(q\,\|\,p(z\mid x)\big)lnp(x)=B(q)+KL(q∥p(z∣x)), with KL≥0\mathrm{KL}\ge0KL≥0 and zero only at the posterior . So the best guess is the posterior, and no score passes ln⁡p(x)\ln p(x)lnp(x).
Insight. Too many stories? Climb inside a smaller family. The climb is cheap, the height is a safe lower bound, and the gap is the price of the family.

Remember: best guess = posterior; smaller family = cheaper guess + a gap.

Way 3 · Everyone guesses alone · The rule

Each update uses the neighbours' current tables as weights

To update coin 2, fix q1q_1q1​ and q3q_3q3​ and use them as weights:

q2(z2) ∝ p(x2∣z2)⏟own flip⋅exp⁡(∑z1q1(z1) ln⁡p(z2∣z1)⏟coin 1’s table as weights)⋅exp⁡(∑z3q3(z3) ln⁡p(z3∣z2)⏟coin 3’s table as weights)q_2(z_2)\ \propto\ \underbrace{p(x_2\mid z_2)}_{\text{own flip}}\cdot\exp\Big(\underbrace{\sum_{z_1}q_1(z_1)\,\ln p(z_2\mid z_1)}_{\text{coin 1's table as weights}}\Big)\cdot\exp\Big(\underbrace{\sum_{z_3}q_3(z_3)\,\ln p(z_3\mid z_2)}_{\text{coin 3's table as weights}}\Big)q2​(z2​) ∝ own flipp(x2​∣z2​)​​⋅exp(coin 1’s table as weightsz1​∑​q1​(z1​)lnp(z2​∣z1​)​​)⋅exp(coin 3’s table as weightsz3​∑​q3​(z3​)lnp(z3​∣z2​)​​)

The weights are fixed numbers, so qqq stays a product.

Way 1: a sum-product messagea sum of tablesall but what coin 2 sent back0.625

Message passing, but not Way 1's: each update raises the score, so the updates converge (stop changing).

Way 3 · Everyone guesses alone · Theorem B

Theorem B: each mean-field update can only raise the score

Theorem B (coordinate ascent). With the other coins fixed, BBB is largest at qt(zt)∝exp⁡(Eothers[ln⁡p(x,z)])q_t(z_t)\propto\exp\big(\mathbb E_{\text{others}}[\ln p(x,z)]\big)qt​(zt​)∝exp(Eothers​[lnp(x,z)]) . Updating the coins in turn never lowers BBB.
Proof in one line: with the others fixed, B=−KL(qt ∥ q~t)+constB=-\mathrm{KL}(q_t\,\|\,\tilde q_t)+\text{const}B=−KL(qt​∥q~​t​)+const, and a KL is ≥0\ge0≥0 .
Insight. One dial at a time, each to its best position: never downhill. It stops where no single dial helps: a local top.

Remember: one coin at a time, always uphill, to a local top.

Way 3 · Everyone guesses alone · Try it

Try it: coin 1 leans to A, so does coin 2's guess go up or down?

Coin 2 showed H: alone, it says A with 0.75. Its neighbours' tables: coin 1 is A with 0.75; coin 3 with 0.5, no opinion. After one update, coin 2's guess of A is …
Answer. Above: 0.839.
  1. Coin 3 adds nothing: a table at 0.5 has no opinion.
  2. Coin 1 adds evidence for A: the friend usually keeps, so coin 2 probably follows coin 1.
  3. The rule adds that evidence to coin 2's own flip: 0.75 rises to 0.839 .

A neighbour's lean counts as extra evidence, so the guesses push each other up.

Way 3 · Everyone guesses alone · By hand

On H, H, T, every update raises the score B

Start from every table at ½ and update coin 1, 2, 3 in turn with the rule : the score rises at every update and converges after three rounds.

It converges below the ceiling ln⁡p(x)\ln p(x)lnp(x), and the converged chances are too sure. All guesses and scores: .

The score never falls and converges fast, but it stops short of ln⁡p(x)\ln p(x)lnp(x).

Way 3 · Everyone guesses alone · The cost

Separate guesses cannot express that two coins tend to agree

Take coins 1 and 2 on the line and compare their four pairs:

  1. the truth gives both B a real chance, because the friend usually keeps;
  2. separate guesses multiply q1q_1q1​ by q2q_2q2​, so cannot say "coin 2 follows coin 1";
  3. to make both A likely, they push both towards A and almost rule out both B.

Too confident means narrower than the truth: weight on fewer stories, a smaller entropy (Week 3), and a coin agreeing with its neighbours gets 0.866 where the truth is 0.8.

Fast and scalable, but narrower than the truth: overconfident.

Way 3 · Everyone guesses alone · A bigger family

Turn the family dial: keep some links inside the guess

  1. All alone: one-coin tables multiplied; 3 numbers.
  2. Line links kept: the guess may say "coin 2 follows coin 1", never the ring link; 5 numbers.
  3. The full table: 7 numbers, every link; the guess can be the truth.

On the line, the line links already close the gap . This is structured mean field.

Bigger family: smaller gap, more work.

Way 3 · Everyone guesses alone · Theorem C

Theorem C: why mean field is too sure

  1. The truth has two peaks: all A (A, A, A and A, A, B) and all B (B, B, B). Between them, a valley of mixed stories.
  2. A product is one tent: it can cover both peaks only by covering the valley too.
  3. Mean field minimizes KL(q∥p)\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)KL(q∥p), which punishes the valley, not a missed peak. So the tent covers the big peak only: B, B, B drops to 0.01. Too sure.
  4. The other direction KL(p∥q)\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)KL(p∥q) punishes a missed peak: both peaks, the true chances. But it needs the truth.
Same formula, qqq and ppp swapped: KL(q∥p)=∑zqln⁡qp\mathrm{KL}(\textcolor{#c86400}{q}\|p)=\sum_z \textcolor{#c86400}{q}\ln\frac{\textcolor{#c86400}{q}}{p}KL(q∥p)=∑z​qlnpq​, weighted by the guess, so a peak the guess leaves out costs nothing; KL(p∥q)=∑zpln⁡pq\mathrm{KL}(\textcolor{#07843a}{p}\|q)=\sum_z \textcolor{#07843a}{p}\ln\frac{\textcolor{#07843a}{p}}{q}KL(p∥q)=∑z​plnqp​, weighted by the truth, so a missed peak costs a lot.

One tent, two peaks: mean field covers the big one and calls it certain.

Way 3 · Everyone guesses alone · Let the truth judge, locally

Let the truth judge, one link at a time

  1. Theorem C: the truth judging, KL(p∥q)\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)KL(p∥q), needs the whole posterior: impossible.
  2. But it can judge one link at a time: replace that link by two one-coin tables, chosen so that, everything else fixed, the two coins' chances match the true link's.
  3. Go round the links until the tables stop changing. This is expectation propagation.

The truth still judges, one link at a time.

Way 3 · Everyone guesses alone · The result

On our coins, this is exactly Way 4

  1. On the line: the exact chances.
  2. On the ring: 0.787, the number of messages in a circle (all coins: ).
  3. Because matching two coins' chances under one true link is exactly what a message does.
coin 1's chance of Alinering
the truth0.80.75
one link at a time (expectation propagation)0.80.787
messages in a circle (Way 4)0.80.787
Insight. The guess judges all at once (Way 3); the truth judges one link at a time (Way 4): the two directions of KL, made local.

Two directions of KL, two ways out.

Way 3 · Everyone guesses alone · Theorem E

Theorem E: variational EM climbs the score, not the likelihood

Theorem E (variational EM). Alternate a mean-field guess step and the count step: each raises BBB. But ln⁡p(x)=B+gap\ln p(x)=B+\text{gap}lnp(x)=B+gap and the gap moves with θ\thetaθ, so ln⁡p(x)\ln p(x)lnp(x) can fall. With the exact guess the gap is 0: Theorem 4 .

H, H, T, T: one round raises BBB but lowers ln⁡p(x)\ln p(x)lnp(x) from −2.936 to −2.967 .

  1. Guess step: labels too sure, so the floor sits far below the house.
  2. Count step: the habits move to where the floor is high.
  3. The floor rose; the house dipped.
Insight. We climb the floor, not the house, so the habits drift to where the family fits well.

Remember: exact guess, the likelihood rises; approximate guess, only the score rises.

Way 3 · Everyone guesses alone · Next

Way 4: pass messages even when the coins form a circle

The messages of Way 1 were exact on a line. What happens if we pass them around a circle?

Way 4 keeps the links between coins that Way 3 drops.

Way 4 · Pass messages in a circle · Idea

On a line, messages stop at the ends; on a circle, they return

We pass the same messages around the circle repeatedly until they converge.

On a circle, a coin's own evidence returns to it and is counted twice.

Way 4 · Pass messages in a circle · The rule

A message carries a coin's news, except the receiver's own

Take coin 2's message to coin 3. It combines:

  1. coin 2's own flip;
  2. the messages coin 2 received from its other neighbours, here coin 1;
  3. not coin 3's message, because coin 3 already knows that news.
μ2→3(z3)=∑z2p(z3∣z2) p(x2∣z2) μ1→2(z2)\mu_{2\to3}(z_3)=\sum_{z_2}p(z_3\mid z_2)\,p(x_2\mid z_2)\,\mu_{1\to2}(z_2)μ2→3​(z3​)=∑z2​​p(z3​∣z2​)p(x2​∣z2​)μ1→2​(z2​) — the sum-product rule

Each coin's guess = own flip × all messages received, rescaled to sum to 1.

This is loopy belief propagation: the sum-product rule on a graph with cycles.

Way 4 · Pass messages in a circle · What we get

On a circle, converged messages give an approximate answer

On a line, the messages are exact . On a circle, we use the same rule anyway:

  1. Start every message at "no information" (12,12\tfrac12,\tfrac1221​,21​).
  2. Update all messages with the rule, round after round.
  3. Stop when they have converged, and read off each coin's guess.

The answer is approximate: a coin's own evidence returns round the circle and is counted again. The messages need not converge.

Fast and usually accurate, but without a guarantee.

Way 4 · Pass messages in a circle · Theorem D

Theorem D: on one circle, the messages pick the right coin

Margin = chance of A − chance of B. Echo eee: send coin 1's margin once round the circle. Each link keeps only keep − switch = ½ of it, each flip trims it a little; the fraction that comes back is the echo. Our ring: e=0.07e=0.07e=0.07.

Theorem D (one circle, two-valued coins). The messages converge, and at every coin true margin=1−e1+e×the messages’ margin.\text{true margin}=\frac{1-e}{1+e}\times\text{the messages' margin}.true margin=1+e1−e​×the messages’ margin.
  1. The factor is positive: same winner.
  2. Coins that agree, e>0e>0e>0: too sure. Coins that switch, e<0e<0e<0: not sure enough.
  3. Faint echo, e≈0e\approx0e≈0: nearly exact.

Our ring: factor 1−0.071+0.07=0.87\tfrac{1-0.07}{1+0.07}=0.871+0.071−0.07​=0.87 .

Remember: on one circle the messages pick the right coin; only their confidence is off, by the echo.

Way 4 · Pass messages in a circle · Insight

Insight: each link shrinks the echo, or flips its sign

  1. Coin 1's margin goes round the circle. Each link multiplies it by keep − switch.
  2. Keep ¾: ×½ per link. After 3 links only ⅛ comes back: a faint echo, small error. After 8 links, almost nothing.
  3. Keep 0.05: ×(−0.9) per link. After 3 links −0.73 comes back: a strong echo pointing the wrong way, large error.

The echo and the error for circles of 3 to 8 coins: .

Long circles or weak links: faint echo, accurate messages. Frequent switching: reversed echo, unreliable messages.

Can we trust it? · The cost

What each way costs for n coins with K values

Count the numbers each way must touch before it answers once:

waywork3 coins, K = 2300 coins, K = 2
list every storyKnK^nKn stories8more than atoms in the universe
1 messages along a linen K2n\,K^2nK2 per pass121 200
2 act it outn Kn\,KnK per sweep6600
3 everyone guesses alonen Kn\,KnK per round6600
4 messages in a circlelinks ×K2\times K^2×K2 per round121 200

With 300 coins on a ring, only the last three are possible: a line needs a line, and 23002^{300}2300 stories cannot be listed.

Listing grows with the power; the ways out grow with the count.

Can we trust it? · Error against compute

Bias you cannot shrink, noise you can

  1. Approximations (Ways 3, 4) carry a fixed bias and no noise: more rounds do not help.
  2. Sampling (Way 2) carries no bias, but noise that shrinks like 1/sweeps1/\sqrt{\text{sweeps}}1/sweeps​.
  3. So sampling wins once you can afford about 300 sweeps here; with fewer, the approximation wins.

Little time: approximate. Much time: sample.

Can we trust it? · An experiment

The stronger the links, the more both approximations drift

Take the ring over H, H, T and vary only the keep chance of every link. Listing the 8 stories gives coin 1 the exact chance 0.75 at every keep. Predict: which approximation drifts first?

Mean field drifts first, 0.917 at keep ¾: separate guesses push each other towards A .

Loopy messages drift later, 0.787 at keep ¾: returning news is counted twice .

Weak links: both are close. Strong links: check against sampling or an exact method.

Can we trust it? · The four ways side by side

On the ring, each way trades bias, noise and speed

All four ways on the ring with keep ¾ (the numbers: ):

wayerrorcostguarantee
1 messages along a lineno line herelowexact if no cycle
2 Gibbs samplingrandom ∝1/runs\propto 1/\sqrt{\text{runs}}∝1/runs​slowright on average
3 mean fieldbiased: too surefast, convergesB≤ln⁡p(x)B\le\ln p(x)B≤lnp(x)
4 loopy messagesbiased, smallerfast, may not convergeexact on trees

Ways 3 and 4: bias, no noise, the same wrong answer every run. Way 2: noise, no bias, a new answer every run, right on average.

No way wins everywhere: choose by cycles, link strength and time.

Can we trust it?

Before believing an answer, make three simple checks

Before believing the learned habits:

  1. Try other starting guesses. EM can stop at a poor answer, so start from several and keep the best score.
  2. Names do not matter. A heads 14\tfrac1441​, B heads 34\tfrac3443​ fits H, H, T equally well: two mirror answers are one answer.
  3. Some questions have no answer. With keep 12\tfrac1221​, the flips look like one fair coin, so no method can find heads 34\tfrac3443​ and 14\tfrac1441​.

Trust an answer only after these checks.

Part 1 · Summary

Four ways to guess when there are too many stories

waypicturegoodcost
1pass messages along a lineexact, low costlines only

Next: all four ways on one small example.

Part 2 · One example

How close does each way get on the friend's three flips?

We measure one thing: each coin's chance of being A given H, H, T, against the exact answer.

  1. The line: Way 1 gives the exact answer; we test Ways 2 and 3.
  2. The circle: link coin 3 to coin 1; the 8 stories give the exact answer; we test Ways 2, 3, 4.
  3. The scoreboard: all answers on one chart.

Three coins: few enough to know the exact answer and grade every way.

Example · Line · The exact answer

On the line, the exact answer is 0.8, 0.75 and 0.4

  1. What we compare: for each coin, the chance that it was coin A, given the flips H, H, T.
  2. Where these come from: Way 1 computed them exactly, step by step . Tails at flip 3 makes coin B likelier there.
  3. What they are for: they are the targets. Ways 2 and 3 are graded by how close they come.

The exact answer on the line: the reference for Ways 2 and 3.

Example · Line · Way 2: act it out

Acting the game out matches the exact answer, but wastes runs

  1. Replay the game 2048 times. On average only 240 runs show H, H, T; the other 1808 are thrown away.
  2. Each bar counts the kept runs of one story. Black bars are the stories with coin 2 = A.
  3. Coin 2 is A in 180 of 240 kept runs: chance 0.75, the exact value.

Right on average, but most of the work is discarded.

Example · Line · Way 3: everyone alone

Guessing alone gives 0.866 where the exact answer is 0.8

Press Run: coins 1, 2, 3 update in turn. Orange bars are the separate guesses; green outlines are the exact chances.

Coins 1 and 2 agree, so each supports the other: 0.866 and 0.848 instead of 0.8 and 0.75.

Guessing alone is overconfident where neighbours agree.

Example · Line · Summary

On the line, only guessing alone misses the exact answer

chance of Acoin 1coin 2coin 3verdict
exact (Way 1, messages)0.80.750.4the reference
Way 2, act it out0.80.750.4on average; slow
Way 3, guess alone0.8660.8480.417too confident

Way 4 is not needed here: on a line, messages in a circle are the messages of Way 1.

A line is easy. The real test is a circle.

Example · Circle · Join the ends

Linking coin 3 back to coin 1 makes a circle

  1. The new link uses the same habit: keep ¾, switch ¼.
  2. Way 1 no longer works, because the messages have no starting point.
  3. With three coins we can still list all 8 stories to get the exact answer.

One extra link turns an easy chain into a hard cycle.

Example · Circle · The exact answer

Listing the 8 stories gives the exact chances 0.75, 0.75, 0.55

  1. A story is one choice of coin for each flip, such as A, A, B. Three coins: 8 stories, one bar each.
  2. A story's weight is how likely the friend plays it and shows H, H, T: multiply the start, every keep or switch (the new link included) and the three flips. (× 8192 only makes whole numbers.) Stories where neighbours agree weigh most, because keep ¾ beats switch ¼.
  3. Chance that coin 3 is A = weight of the stories with coin 3 = A (green) ÷ weight of all stories = 264 ÷ 480 = 0.55.

Checking every story is the exact answer; with three coins we can still afford it.

Example · Circle · Way 2: one coin at a time

Redrawing one coin at a time reaches 0.739, 0.732, 0.542

Press Run. One sweep redraws coins 1, 2 and 3 once. Black lines show how often each coin has been A so far; green dashes are the exact chances.

After 1000 sweeps every estimate is within 0.02 of the exact answer.

Example · Circle · Way 3: everyone alone

On the circle, guessing alone gives 0.917 instead of 0.75

Each coin now has two neighbours that agree with it, so each gets more support than on the line.

More links between coins make guessing alone more overconfident.

Example · Circle · Way 4: messages in a circle

Messages around the circle converge to 0.787 instead of 0.75

Press Run: the messages go round the circle until they converge. Blue bars are the messages' guesses; green outlines are the exact chances.

Close but not exact, because some evidence is counted twice.

Example · Circle · Scoreboard

On the circle, sampling and messages are close; guessing alone is not

Each group is one coin. Compare every bar with the green bar, the exact answer.

Largest error: sampling 0.018, messages in a circle 0.037, guessing alone 0.167.

Choose a way by what you can pay: time, a cycle-free graph, or some accuracy.

Part 2 · Next

The same four ways are used in today's artificial intelligence

Replace the coins by sounds, words, image codes or the bits sent to a phone, and the same problem appears.

The same problem appears with many more hidden variables.

Part 3 · In AI today

Each of the four ways runs inside a system you have used

The score and the four ways stay the same; only the hidden variables change.

Part 3 · Way 1 · Speech recognition

Speech recognition used messages passed along a sentence

Take a recording of the word "hello". It matches our coin game:

  1. the hidden coins become the sounds h, e, l, l, o;
  2. the flips become the slices of the recording;
  3. keep or switch becomes stay on a sound or move to the next, so the sounds form a line.

For decades, speech recognizers were trained this way.

Part 3 · Way 2 · Reasoning models

Reasoning models act out solutions and keep the correct ones

Take a maths question with a known answer. It matches acting the game out:

  1. the hidden coins become the steps of a solution, which the data never show;
  2. replaying the game becomes writing many attempts;
  3. keeping the runs that match becomes keeping the attempts with the right answer, then learning from them.

This is Way 2 applied to language models.

Part 3 · Way 3 · Topic models

Topic models let each word guess its topic alone

Take a short document: team, goal, vote, coach, party, wins. It matches everyone guessing alone:

  1. the hidden coins become each word's topic, such as sport or politics;
  2. the flips become the words we read;
  3. each word makes its own guess of its topic, which is fast enough for whole libraries.

Fast enough for millions of documents, but somewhat overconfident.

Part 3 · Way 3 · Coming in Week 10

A network can learn to make the guess in one step

Take a picture. It matches our coin game:

  1. the hidden coins become the picture's hidden code;
  2. our guess qqq is made by a network, the encoder, in one step;
  3. the same score trains it: redraw the picture well and keep the guess simple.

Week 10: the variational autoencoder, which learns the guess with a network.

Part 3 · Way 3 · Coming in Week 11

Image generators raise the same score along a chain

Take a picture that is slowly turned into noise. It matches our coin game:

  1. the hidden coins become the noisy pictures in between;
  2. each noisy picture comes from the one before, so they form a chain, like our line of coins;
  3. learning to remove a little noise at each step raises the same score.

Week 11: diffusion models, trained with the same score.

Part 3 · Way 4 · Your phone

Your phone passes messages in a large network with cycles

Take the bits sent to your phone. They arrive with noise:

  1. the hidden coins become the bits that were sent;
  2. each check says its bits add to an even number; the checks link bits into long cycles;
  3. messages round these cycles correct the noisy bits in a fraction of a second.

Messages in a circle work best when the cycles are long, as in 5G codes.

Summary · The whole story

With too many stories, we score the guess and choose a way

Too many secret stories to check, so a score measures any guess and EM raises it.

  1. Pass messages along a line: exact on a line.
  2. Act it out: correct on average, but slow.
  3. Everyone guesses alone: fast, but overconfident.
  4. Pass messages in a circle: fast and close, not exact.

Before believing an answer: try other starting guesses, names do not matter, and can the data answer at all?

One score, four ways out, three checks.

Check yourself

Check yourself (1 of 2): the score and the messages

1. Our guess scores far below the truth. What does this tell us?
Answer. The guess is far from the true answer: the gap measures exactly this; a perfect guess has no gap.
2. Why can coins in a line pass messages instead of listing every story?
Answer. Each coin depends only on its neighbour, so one message from each side is enough.

Score every guess; use the chain structure when it exists.

Check yourself

Check yourself (2 of 2): acting out and guessing alone

3. Acting out gives an error of about 0.1. How many times as many runs halve it?
Answer. Four times as many, because the error shrinks like one over the square root of the runs.
4. Two linked coins both lean to A. Compared with the truth, the separate guesses for A are usually …
Answer. Higher, because the separate guesses reinforce each other.

Acting out is slow; guessing alone is overconfident.

Appendix · Trust · Proof

On the diagonal, both slopes of ℓ are zero

Recall : ℓ=∑xln⁡[12⋅f(x∣θA)+12⋅f(x∣θB)]\ell=\sum_x\ln\bigl[\tfrac12 \cdot f(x\mid\theta_A)+\tfrac12 \cdot f(x\mid\theta_B)\bigr]ℓ=∑x​ln[21​⋅f(x∣θA​)+21​⋅f(x∣θB​)] with f(x∣t)=thx⋅(1−t)nx−hxf(x\mid t)=t^{h_x}\cdot(1-t)^{n_x-h_x}f(x∣t)=thx​⋅(1−t)nx​−hx​, one coin's chance of record xxx; t^=∑xhx/∑xnx\hat t=\sum_x h_x\big/\sum_x n_xt^=∑x​hx​/∑x​nx​.

Diagonal fact, part 2. (t^,t^)(\hat t,\hat t)(t^,t^) is a stationary point of ℓ\ellℓ: ∂ℓ/∂θA=∂ℓ/∂θB=0\partial\ell/\partial\theta_A=\partial\ell/\partial\theta_B=0∂ℓ/∂θA​=∂ℓ/∂θB​=0 there.
∂ℓ∂θA∣(t,t)=∑x12⋅f′(x∣θA)12⋅f(x∣θA)+12⋅f(x∣θB)∣(t,t)(chain rule for ln⁡; only A’s term has θA)=12⋅∑xf′(x∣t)f(x∣t)(at (t,t) the two halves add to f)=12⋅ddt∑xln⁡f(x∣t)(f′/f=(ln⁡f)′)=0  at t=t^(Theorem 1: best fit = heads/flips)\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\theta_A}\Big|_{(t,t)}&=\sum_x\frac{\tfrac12 \cdot f'(x\mid\theta_A)}{\tfrac12 \cdot f(x\mid\theta_A)+\tfrac12 \cdot f(x\mid\theta_B)}\Big|_{(t,t)}&&(\text{chain rule for }\ln\text{; only A's term has }\theta_A)\\&=\tfrac12\cdot\sum_x\frac{f'(x\mid t)}{f(x\mid t)}&&(\text{at }(t,t)\text{ the two halves add to }f)\\&=\tfrac12\cdot\frac{d}{dt}\sum_x\ln f(x\mid t)&&(f'/f=(\ln f)')\\&=0\ \text{ at }t=\hat t&&\text{(Theorem 1: best fit = heads/flips)}\end{aligned}∂θA​∂ℓ​​(t,t)​​=x∑​21​⋅f(x∣θA​)+21​⋅f(x∣θB​)21​⋅f′(x∣θA​)​​(t,t)​=21​⋅x∑​f(x∣t)f′(x∣t)​=21​⋅dtd​x∑​lnf(x∣t)=0  at t=t^​​(chain rule for ln; only A’s term has θA​)(at (t,t) the two halves add to f)(f′/f=(lnf)′)(Theorem 1: best fit = heads/flips)​

In words: on the diagonal each slope is half the slope of one coin's log-likelihood, which is flat at t^\hat tt^. The same steps give ∂ℓ/∂θB=0\partial\ell/\partial\theta_B=0∂ℓ/∂θB​=0.

Why it matters: stationary is not the same as best: whether (t^,t^)(\hat t,\hat t)(t^,t^) is a peak or a trap depends on how ℓ\ellℓ curves across the diagonal.

The resting point on the diagonal is flat in every direction, but not necessarily a peak.

Appendix · Trust · Worked details

Two identical coins sit on a saddle

Quick recap. Two mirror peaks ; between them sit two identical fair coins, (θA,θB)=(12,12)(\theta_A,\theta_B)=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)(θA​,θB​)=(21​,21​). Saddle = highest in one direction, lowest in another. Along: move both coins the same way; across: move them apart.
StepNumberWhy
1. Middleℓ=−4.159\ell=-4.159ℓ=−4.159Each record has chance 14\tfrac1441​: 3⋅ln⁡143\cdot\ln\tfrac143⋅ln41​.
2. Along3⋅ln⁡(14−d2)3\cdot\ln(\tfrac14-d^2)3⋅ln(41​−d2)Any move lowers ℓ\ellℓ: highest at the middle.
3. Across≈−4.159+4⋅d2\approx-4.159+4\cdot d^2≈−4.159+4⋅d2Any move raises ℓ\ellℓ: lowest at the middle.

Highest along, lowest across: a saddle, a worse fit than the mirror peaks.

Ways 3 and 4The first mean-field sweeps by hand; the Bethe free energy formula; the most likely state as a linear program.
Can we trust it?The three answers; mirror peaks; identical coins; the saddle; restarts; the counting test; Teicher; two settings, same data.

Everything here is the full version of a claim the lecture makes in one line.

Appendix · Way 2 · Lecture 5's two coins

Hard EM replaces each soft label by the single most likely hidden value

Definition (hard EM). At the guess θt\theta_tθt​, for each record nnn:
E-step: take the most likely hidden value (ties by a fixed rule)
z^(n)=arg⁡max⁡zpθt(z∣x(n))=arg⁡max⁡zpθt(x(n),z)\hat z^{(n)}=\arg\max_z p_{\theta_t}\big(z\mid x^{(n)}\big)=\arg\max_z p_{\theta_t}\big(x^{(n)},z\big)z^(n)=argzmax​pθt​​(z∣x(n))=argzmax​pθt​​(x(n),z)
(same denominator pθt(x(n))p_{\theta_t}(x^{(n)})pθt​​(x(n))), and use the label 111 on z^(n)\hat z^{(n)}z^(n), 000 elsewhere.
M-step: θt+1=arg⁡max⁡θ∑nln⁡pθ(x(n),z^(n))\theta_{t+1}=\arg\max_\theta\sum_n\ln p_\theta\big(x^{(n)},\hat z^{(n)}\big)θt+1​=argmaxθ​∑n​lnpθ​(x(n),z^(n)), maximum likelihood with these told labels.

It is Monte Carlo EM with one "draw" per record that is always the most likely value, as in k-means .

Why it matters: no normalizing sum and no random draws are needed, but the label is no longer the posterior, so Theorem 4's increase is lost: the log-likelihood can fall (Appendix, Way 2 ).

Hard EM rounds each posterior to 0 or 1; it is cheap, but it throws the uncertainty away.

Appendix · Way 2 · Lecture 5's two coins

Replay the game and keep the runs that match: the kept runs follow the posterior

Proposition (replay and keep) applied to HH, one record of Lecture 5's two-coin game (pick A or B with chance ½, flip it twice). Replay the game at the guess θA=34,θB=14\theta_A=\tfrac34,\theta_B=\tfrac14θA​=43​,θB​=41​ and keep a run only if it shows HH. Shown: 32 replays at their expected counts; a fair toss sends 32⋅12=1632\cdot\tfrac12=1632⋅21​=16 runs to each coin.

No sum was computed: we only ran the game forward and compared. Its cost: 32−10=2232-10=2232−10=22 of the 32 runs are thrown away. The keep rate 10/32=9/32+1/3210/32=9/32+1/3210/32=9/32+1/32 is exactly p(HH)p(\text{HH})p(HH), which we never computed. So rare records waste most runs.

Kept runs show A : B = 9 : 1, so each kept run's coin is a posterior draw: A with chance 0.9.

Appendix · Way 2 · Lecture 5's two coins

Theorem 7 on HT: ten draws give noise 0.158, and four times the draws halve it

Theorem 7 applied to HT. At θA=34,θB=14\theta_A=\tfrac34,\theta_B=\tfrac14θA​=43​,θB​=41​ the posterior of A given HT is q=12q=\tfrac12q=21​ (recall) ; we drew m=10m=10m=10 times.

standard deviation=q⋅(1−q)/mTheorem 7=12⋅12/10=0.15814/10=0.025, 0.025=0.158\begin{aligned} \text{standard deviation}&=\sqrt{q\cdot(1-q)/m} && \text{Theorem 7}\\ &=\sqrt{\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12/10}=0.158 && \tfrac14/10=0.025,\ \sqrt{0.025}=0.158 \end{aligned}standard deviation​=q⋅(1−q)/m​=21​⋅21​/10​=0.158​​Theorem 741​/10=0.025, 0.025​=0.158​

Ten draws typically miss by about 0.16, so HT's 0.7 (posterior 0.5) is ordinary luck, which the new guess inherits: θA=0.781\theta_A=0.781θA​=0.781, not EM's 0.767 .

Hard EM instead: round, do not drawGive each record wholly to its likelier coin: HH → A, HT → A (tie), TT → B. Counting then gives θA=34\theta_A=\tfrac34θA​=43​, θB=0\theta_B=0θB​=0, and the labels stay A, A, B: hard EM is stuck. Its fit ℓ=−4.268\ell=-4.268ℓ=−4.268 is below the start's −4.000-4.000−4.000 : rounding throws away information (all steps: Appendix ).

Draws add noise ∝1/m\propto1/\sqrt m∝1/m​ that more draws remove; rounding to one coin can get stuck.

Appendix · Way 4 · Definition

The Bethe free energy, and the most likely state

Bethe free energy (pairwise model; btb_tbt​, bstb_{st}bst​ = single and pairwise beliefs that agree on their overlaps): FBethe=−∑factors aEba[ln⁡fa]⏟energy − (∑links stH(bst)−∑t(dt−1) H(bt))⏟entropy from piecesF_{\text{Bethe}}=\underbrace{-\sum_{\text{factors }a}\mathbb E_{b_a}[\ln f_a]}_{\text{energy}}\ -\ \underbrace{\Big(\sum_{\text{links }st}H(b_{st})-\sum_t(d_t-1)\,H(b_t)\Big)}_{\text{entropy from pieces}}FBethe​=energy−factors a∑​Eba​​[lnfa​]​​ − entropy from pieces(links st∑​H(bst​)−t∑​(dt​−1)H(bt​))​​ HHH = entropy, dtd_tdt​ = number of links at ttt. On a tree this equals −ln⁡pθ(x)-\ln p_\theta(x)−lnpθ​(x) at the exact marginals.

Most likely state. Asking for the single most likely hidden sequence instead relaxes to a linear program over the same locally consistent beliefs; it is exact on trees, and max-product messages are closely related (Wainwright and Jordan, 2008, ch. 8).

BP's beliefs are where this free energy is flat; on a tree that is the exact answer.

Appendix · Can we trust it? · Details

The coin fit has two mirror-image peaks

Can a learned θ=(θA,θB)\theta=(\theta_A,\theta_B)θ=(θA​,θB​) be trusted? Colour the log-likelihood ℓ\ellℓ of Lecture 5's records HH, HT, TT over every pair of heads chances.

Two equally high peaks appear, mirror images across the diagonal θA=θB\theta_A=\theta_BθA​=θB​ (identical coins), with an orange point between them.

Three questions:
1. Why are the peaks mirror images?
2. Can EM get stuck between them?
3. Can the data always pick one answer?

Before trusting a fit, ask whether a different setting fits just as well.

Appendix · Can we trust it? · Details

Renaming the coins never changes the likelihood

Label-switching lemma. If the friend picks each coin with chance 12\tfrac1221​, then ℓ(θA,θB)=ℓ(θB,θA)\ell(\theta_A,\theta_B)=\ell(\theta_B,\theta_A)ℓ(θA​,θB​)=ℓ(θB​,θA​) for every pair of heads chances.

Write f(x∣t)f(x\mid t)f(x∣t) for the chance that one coin with heads chance ttt produces record xxx.

ℓ(θA,θB)=∑xln⁡pθ(x)(independent records)=∑xln⁡[12⋅f(x∣θA)+12⋅f(x∣θB)](sum over hidden coin z)=∑xln⁡[12⋅f(x∣θB)+12⋅f(x∣θA)](addition commutes)=ℓ(θB,θA)(line 2, names swapped)\begin{aligned}\ell(\theta_A,\theta_B)&=\sum_x\ln p_\theta(x)&&\text{(independent records)}\\&=\sum_x\ln\bigl[\tfrac12 \cdot f(x\mid\theta_A)+\tfrac12 \cdot f(x\mid\theta_B)\bigr]&&\text{(sum over hidden coin }z)\\&=\sum_x\ln\bigl[\tfrac12 \cdot f(x\mid\theta_B)+\tfrac12 \cdot f(x\mid\theta_A)\bigr]&&\text{(addition commutes)}\\&=\ell(\theta_B,\theta_A)&&\text{(line 2, names swapped)}\end{aligned}ℓ(θA​,θB​)​=x∑​lnpθ​(x)=x∑​ln[21​⋅f(x∣θA​)+21​⋅f(x∣θB​)]=x∑​ln[21​⋅f(x∣θB​)+21​⋅f(x∣θA​)]=ℓ(θB​,θA​)​​(independent records)(sum over hidden coin z)(addition commutes)(line 2, names swapped)​

Why it matters: every peak (a,b)(a,b)(a,b) has an equally high mirror peak (b,a)(b,a)(b,a). With an unknown pick chance π\piπ, the same steps give ℓ(π,θA,θB)=ℓ(1−π,θB,θA)\ell(\pi,\theta_A,\theta_B)=\ell(1-\pi,\theta_B,\theta_A)ℓ(π,θA​,θB​)=ℓ(1−π,θB​,θA​).

Names are labels, not facts: the data see only the unordered pair of coins.

Appendix · Can we trust it? · Details

Across the diagonal, ℓ can curve upward: a saddle

Saddle test. Along the diagonal, ℓ(t,t)\ell(t,t)ℓ(t,t) is one coin's log-likelihood, largest at t=t^t=\hat tt=t^ (Theorem 1) . Across it, ℓ\ellℓ rises if ∑xf′′(x∣t^)/f(x∣t^)>0\sum_x f''(x\mid\hat t)/f(x\mid\hat t)\gt0∑x​f′′(x∣t^)/f(x∣t^)>0; then (t^,t^)(\hat t,\hat t)(t^,t^) is a saddle.
ℓ(t^+d, t^−d)≈ℓ(t^,t^)+d22⋅∑xf′′(x∣t^)f(x∣t^)\ell(\hat t+d,\,\hat t-d)\approx\ell(\hat t,\hat t)+\dfrac{d^2}{2}\cdot\sum_x\dfrac{f''(x\mid\hat t)}{f(x\mid\hat t)}ℓ(t^+d,t^−d)≈ℓ(t^,t^)+2d2​⋅∑x​f(x∣t^)f′′(x∣t^)​ (averaging ±d\pm d±d cancels the ddd terms)

In words: along the diagonal it is a top, across it a dip. By the diagonal fact , EM started there stops there anyway.

A saddle is a worse fit, and a symmetric start makes EM stop exactly there.

Appendix · Can we trust it? · Details

Random restarts reach the top with high probability

Theorem 4 : ℓ\ellℓ never goes down, but EM may stop at a lower peak or a saddle. The same holds for the floor of variational EM and for where loopy BP converges.

Restart principle. Run from KKK independent random starts; keep the run with the largest ℓ\ellℓ (or the largest ELBO).

If a random start reaches the top with chance ρ>0\rho\gt0ρ>0, all KKK runs miss with chance (1−ρ)K→0\cO{(1-\rho)^K\to0}(1−ρ)K→0.

Several random starts escape saddles and lower peaks; keep the best score.

Appendix · Can we trust it? · Details

More unknowns than free numbers means no unique fit

Question 3: can the data always pick one answer?

Theorem 8 (counting test). If a model has more unknowns than one record's distribution has free numbers (its chances, minus one because they sum to 1), then a whole curve of settings fits equally well.

Coins: 3 unknowns π=p(A), θA, θB\pi=p(A),\ \theta_A,\ \theta_Bπ=p(A), θA​, θB​; two flips give p(0),p(1),p(2)p(0),p(1),p(2)p(0),p(1),p(2), summing to 1: 2 free numbers <3\lt3<3.

Why: 3 knobs, but the data read only 2 dials. One direction of turning the knobs leaves both dials unchanged.

Count before you fit: no algorithm can choose between settings the data cannot tell apart.

Appendix · Can we trust it? · Details

With three flips per record, the two coins are pinned down

Theorem (Teicher). With three or more flips per record (and two really different coins), the data pin down π,θA,θB\pi,\theta_A,\theta_Bπ,θA​,θB​: only renaming A ↔ B is left.

In words: two flips leave a curve of equal fits; three flips leave only a setting and its mirror.

Teicher, 1963; Allman, Matias & Rhodes, 2009.

Observe more per record, and the curve of equal fits shrinks back to two mirror peaks.

Appendix · Example · Learning the habits

Counting with those guesses makes the flips more likely

One count step replaces the first guess of the habits:

  1. coin A's heads chance: 34\tfrac3443​ becomes 0.795;
  2. coin B's heads chance: 14\tfrac1441​ becomes 0.429;
  3. the chance to keep the coin: 34\tfrac3443​ becomes 0.7.

One round of Baum–Welch improves the fit, as every EM round does.

Appendix · Way 2 · Worked details

One redraw, worked: coin 2 becomes A with chance 0.75

Slide : the current story is A, A, B over H, H, T on the ring with keep ¾. Coin 2 is redrawn from the three things that touch it; each value of coin 2 gets a weight, the product of the three.

if coin 2 is …coin 1 is A, so the move 1 → 2 iscoin 3 is B, so the move 2 → 3 iscoin 2 shows Hweight
Akeep: ¾switch: ¼A shows H: ¾¾ · ¼ · ¾ = 9/64
Bswitch: ¼keep: ¾B shows H: ¼¼ · ¾ · ¼ = 3/64
Coin 2 is redrawn as A with chance 9 ÷ (9 + 3) = 0.75, and as B with chance 0.25: the same three squares as the formula p(z2∣z1,z3,x2)∝p(z2∣z1) p(z3∣z2) p(x2∣z2)p(z_2\mid z_1,z_3,x_2)\propto p(z_2\mid z_1)\,p(z_3\mid z_2)\,p(x_2\mid z_2)p(z2​∣z1​,z3​,x2​)∝p(z2​∣z1​)p(z3​∣z2​)p(x2​∣z2​).

Then redraw coin 3 the same way from coin 2, coin 1 and its flip T; then coin 1; then coin 2 again, and so on. Each redraw uses only the current values of the two neighbours, so a redraw costs three factors however long the circle is.

Only the squares that touch coin 2 enter the redraw: three factors, two weights, one chance.

Appendix · Way 2 · Worked details

Counting the kept runs gives Baum–Welch's habits

Slide : the 240 kept runs of H, H, T , each counted like kept run 1 (coin A: 2 flips, 2 heads; coin B: 1 flip, 0 heads; kept once, switched once), then added up.

habitcountof whichnew habit
coin A's heads chance468 flips372 heads372 ÷ 468 = 0.795
coin B's heads chance252 flips108 heads108 ÷ 252 = 0.429
chance to keep the coin480 moves336 keeps336 ÷ 480 = 0.7

These are the habits of Baum–Welch's count step : the kept runs come in the right proportions, so counting them is the same as weighting every story by its chance.

Count the kept runs and you have the count step, no sum over stories needed.

Theorem E on four flips H, H, T, T: one mean-field guess step with the habits before, then one count step with those soft labels; the score BBB is taken with the same guess before and after.

four flips H, H, T, Tstart AkeepA headsB headsscore BBBln⁡p(x)\ln p(x)lnp(x)
before0.3630.8200.7440.365−3.416−2.936

  1. Guess step: mean field with the habits before gives each flip a soft label, the chance of A: 0.354, 0.252, 0.053, 0.094.
  2. Count step: those labels, counted as Baum–Welch counts , give the habits after one round.
  3. Compare: the score rises by 0.128, as Theorem E promises, but only because the gap ln⁡p(x)−B\ln p(x)-Blnp(x)−B shrank from 0.480 to 0.321; the likelihood itself falls by 0.031. With the exact guess the gap would be 0 and ln⁡p(x)\ln p(x)lnp(x) could not fall .

A higher score is not a higher likelihood when the gap moves with the habits.

Each link multiplies a lean by keep − switch = ½, so the echo fades link by link, and the error fades with it. The circle of 3 is the worst case; by 8 coins the messages are exact to three decimals.
